text: {"answer":"A systematic review and meta-analysis reports that creatine supplementation enhanced measures of memory performance in healthy individuals, with the effect described as especially evident in older adults aged 66-76 years [60e469276e13#0]. A narrative review of creatine monohydrate in older adults likewise lists memory among the cognitive benefits observed in accumulating research, though it notes benefits are primarily seen when combined with exercise training [51a9f6b43450#1]. The contradicting evidence is a single six-week trial in healthy young adults, which found creatine at moderate or high doses had no significant effect on cognitive performance [3d02a7e7575a#1]. This study concerned young adults rather than older people, so it does not directly undercut the older-adult finding, but it shows that benefits are not universal. Another review on cognition and memory in older adults describes the potential and challenges of creatine, indicating the evidence base is not yet settled [47c94ec99e80#0]. Overall, the evidence favors a memory benefit in older adults, but it rests on a limited number of trials and reviews.","confidence":62,"one_line":"Evidence leans toward creatine improving memory in healthy older adults, though it is limited and a young-adult trial found no effect."}
